summary: Defines the multipart/form-data media type, used to send a set of values from a filled-in form, including file uploads, in one message. It obsoletes RFC 2388 and is the basis of HTML file uploads.

eli5.summary: When you fill out a form and attach a photo, this is how everything goes in one envelope with separate labeled sections.

questions: how do file uploads work in html forms
how does multipart form data work
what is the boundary in multipart/form-data
how are multiple files sent in a form field
subtitle: The message format browsers use to send filled-in forms and file uploads in one body, one labeled part per field.

tldr.problem: A filled-in form can hold typed text, hidden values and whole files, and needs to travel as one message with each value kept separate and labeled.
tldr.mechanism: The multipart/form-data media type splits the body into parts separated by a boundary. Each part has a Content-Disposition of form-data with the field name, an optional filename, and an optional Content-Type.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2388, tidies up how non-ASCII names, multiple files and character sets are handled, and deprecates Content-Transfer-Encoding.

today: RFC 7578 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2388. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of multipart/form-data.

sections.title: What multipart/form-data Is For
sections.content:
A user is presented with a form, fills it in with typed text, generated input or files they select, and the data is sent to a receiving application. The multipart/form-data definition comes from that scenario, first set out in RFC 1867 and then incorporated into HTML 3.2, where the form data is sent by HTTP or electronic mail. The RFC says the representation is widely implemented in web browsers and web servers.

The media type is also used for forms that are not HTML, for transports other than mail or HTTP, and in applications with no user filling out a form. So the RFC defines a general syntax and semantics, with web-specific rules noted in context.

RFC 7578 obsoletes RFC 2388.
sections.eli5: When you send a form, everything you typed or attached has to fit in one package. This RFC says how to pack it so the other side can unpack it correctly.

sections.title: Parts, Boundaries and Headers
sections.content:
The format follows the multipart MIME model of RFC 2046. A body is a series of parts separated by a boundary. The boundary delimiter is built from CRLF, -- and the value of the boundary parameter, which is now a required parameter. The delimiter MUST NOT appear inside any part, and the parameter value often needs quotes in the Content-Type header field.

Each part MUST contain a Content-Disposition header field with disposition type form-data and a name parameter holding the original field name, for example Content-Disposition: form-data; name="user". For file contents, a filename parameter SHOULD be supplied, though it is not mandatory when the name is unavailable, meaningless or private.

A part MAY have a Content-Type, which defaults to text/plain. File data SHOULD be labeled with an appropriate media type if known, or application/octet-stream. No other Content- header fields are supported: they MUST NOT be included and MUST be ignored, apart from Content-Transfer-Encoding in limited circumstances.
sections.eli5: Each bag in the box has a tag with the question it answers. A special line of dashes and a secret word marks where one bag ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Files and Multiple Files
sections.content:
When a part carries a file, the receiver must be careful with filename. The requirements from RFC 2183 for a receiving mail user agent apply: do not use the file name blindly, adjust it to local file system conventions if needed, and ignore any directory path in it.

A form field may hold several files. RFC 2388 suggested a nested multipart/mixed part, and that is now deprecated. To match widely deployed implementations, multiple files MUST be sent as separate parts that all share the same name. General-purpose receivers, such as parsing libraries, SHOULD also still accept the older nested method.
sections.eli5: If you attach three photos to one question, each photo gets its own bag, and all three bags carry the same question on the tag.

sections.title: Character Sets and Non-ASCII Text
sections.content:
MIME header fields normally allow only US-ASCII, which makes non-ASCII field names and file names awkward. RFC 7578 recommends that form authors avoid non-ASCII field names, since the names are generally not visible to users. If they cannot be avoided, UTF-8 SHOULD be used throughout. File names normally visible to users MAY be percent-encoded, but the filename* method from RFC 5987 MUST NOT be used.

For text values, a charset parameter on a text/plain part MAY name the encoding. Many implementations do not send one and rely on a default charset. A hidden form entry named _charset_ sets that default when it is present. HTML 5 picks the form-charset from, in order: the _charset_ field, the form's accept-charset attribute, the document's encoding if it is US-ASCII compatible, and otherwise UTF-8. Text outside ASCII MAY then be sent directly in the form-charset.

Parsers should expect variety. Some generators followed RFC 2388 and used the RFC 2047 encoded-word method, while others used RFC 2231, plain UTF-8, or the form-charset. Interpreting a body may therefore require knowing the form's charset when none is supplied.

Senders SHOULD NOT generate any part with a Content-Transfer-Encoding header field. The old advice to use it, for example with quoted-printable, is deprecated where binary data is supported, as in HTTP.
sections.eli5: Different countries write with different alphabets. The form says which alphabet it is using, and if it does not say, everyone is expected to guess UTF-8 or follow the form's own page.

sections.title: Order, Duplicates and Older Formats
sections.content:
Form processors given a form with a defined order SHOULD send results back in that order. Intermediaries MUST NOT reorder them, and parts with identical field names MUST NOT be coalesced.

Many web applications still use application/x-www-form-urlencoded, which is compact but cannot label data with a content type or charset. Browsers now generate multipart/form-data, but a receiving application might still need to support both. There is no built-in way to tie a body to the form that produced it, which the RFC says is intentional. Applications usually use a per-form processing resource, such as the HTML ACTION attribute, or a hidden field.

The RFC admits that the format is verbose when there are many short fields, though in most cases this overhead is not significant.
sections.eli5: Answers go back in the same order as the questions, and two questions with the same name still get two separate answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Form data often holds confidential or personally identifying information, and browser auto-fill features might be used to trick users into sending it unknowingly. multipart/form-data offers no integrity, confidentiality or other protections; those must come from the applications and the transport.

Files can reach the server with arbitrary executable content, so precautions against malicious content are necessary. Receivers must not overwrite files in their own file space when interpreting filename. On the sending side, scripts that fill in forms and could include a user's local files need extra caution, because a script might send one of those files to another address.
sections.eli5: The box has no lock. Anything private you put in is only safe if the delivery is safe, and whoever opens it should not trust what is inside or the label on the bag.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2388
sections.content:
The main changes from RFC 2388 are these.

  • Non-ASCII field names: the RFC 2047 method is no longer recommended. Senders are advised to send UTF-8 field names directly and file names in the form-charset.
  • Multiple files in one field now each get their own top-level part with the same name, instead of nested multipart/mixed.
  • The _charset_ convention and an explicit form-data charset are documented, and boundary is now a required parameter.
  • Field ordering and same-name fields, which were undefined before, are now addressed.

The RFC also lists editorial changes, such as updated references and moving the outline of form processing into the introduction.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what changed since the old rulebook: clearer rules for other alphabets, one bag per file, and a required secret word.

Xavier

Content-Type: text/plain

...file contents...
--AaB03x--
